6d52bae03f8e:
The Presentation of the Lord – icon painted on glass

The theme of this icon (model: Nicula, second half of the 19th century) is "the Presentation in the Temple", an event closely linked to the theme of purification and redemption.
Forty days after Christmas we celebrate the Presentation of the Lord.

Jesus Christ is brought to the Temple in Jerusalem by the Holy Virgin Mary and Joseph the Righteous to fulfil the rules of the old Law (the Law of Moses), which required that, 40 days after the birth of a first child, the child be presented at the Temple in Jerusalem with an offering to redeem the firstborn, who in fact belonged to God. The offering was a lamb and a dove. The poor, who had no lamb, could bring two young pigeons (one of which symbolised the offering of thanks to God for the gift received, while the other was the price of redemption for the child, who would otherwise have had to dedicate his life to the service of God).
13e0ea530c3f:
~ Saint George the Martyr – icon painted on glass ~
The theme of this icon is Saint George the Great Martyr, in a special iconographic depiction (model: Țara Oltului, first half of the 19th century).

This Saint was a Roman soldier of Greek origin and an officer in the Guard of the Roman emperor Diocletian. He was sentenced to death for refusing to renounce the Christian faith. As a Christian martyr he later became one of the most venerated saints of Christianity, and was especially venerated by the crusaders. Saint George is remembered by almost all the traditional Churches, usually on 23 April. He is considered the patron of many countries, regions and cities all over the world.

74c9d39148a9:
Jesus – the True Vine (model: Șcheii Brașovului, early 19th century) – icon painted on glass
~The iconographic scene shows the risen Jesus Christ before the Cross (standing on the Holy Table of the Altar), and from His side grows a vine (full of grapes), which Christ's hand presses straight into the Holy Chalice. From the image one can easily deduce that the icon does not aim to highlight the metaphor of the vine, frequent in the New Testament writings, but what we find in the Holy Chalice, namely: "in the form of the wine flowing from the grapes is the very Blood of Christ (truly), for the vine grows and is nourished from His side. And on the Holy Table of the Altar lies the very body of the risen Christ".~

7d9f2fca2310:
Icon on glass –
”The Sorrowful Mother of God”

In the painting of icons on glass, it can be said that this type of composition (the theme of the Sorrowful Mother of God) was born in Transylvania. This theme is (in fact) the most frequent in Transylvanian iconography.
The version that became classic throughout Transylvania is the one in which the Mother of God stands with her hands joined in prayer, looking towards the cross of the crucifixion, painted in miniature in the background.
One of the versions of this theme (and one of the most beautiful) was painted in Arpașu de Jos in 1877; after its model I painted the icon whose photo you see here: a traditional Romanian icon made in the style of the icons painted by the Transylvanian icon painters of the 18th–19th centuries, respecting the techniques of this art form.

About the icon:

Painted on glass in several layers, using tempera and gold leaf, over a pen-and-ink drawing made after the original model.
The ink drawing is fixed and protected with varnish, and the finished painting has a protective layer.
The stained fir frame is also handmade.
Icon size: 21x29 cm (without frame); 27.55x35.5 cm (with frame)

b750da475085:
Saints Peter and Paul – icon on glass (model: Transylvanian workshop, early 19th century)

The theme of this icon is the Apostles Peter and Paul.

In Orthodox iconography, Saints Peter and Paul (the first and the last among the Apostles) stand for the Church, or the communion of Israel (Peter) with all the peoples of the world (Paul).
The model of the Church held up by the two saints illustrates the words of Jesus: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My Church"

About the icon:
This traditional Romanian icon is made in the style of the icons painted by the Transylvanian icon painters of the 18th–19th centuries, respecting the techniques of this art form (ink drawing with a calligraphy pen; painting in egg-emulsion tempera; decorative elements in gold leaf).
It is a small icon (with a stand on the frame and hangers), perfect as a special gift (painted glass: 12x17 cm; framed icon: 17x22 cm).

9942695884c5:
Saint Nicholas – icon painted on glass

Most of the icons painted by the unique and wonderful Transylvanian icon painters of the 18th–19th centuries are made like fantastic painted fairy tales, in which the Saints "meet" harmoniously with earthly people caught in their daily activities. This icon too (model: Cârțișoara, second half of the 18th century) is like a gentle story told "by the fireside": Saint Nicholas is shown as a high prelate, holding the Scripture in his right hand and blessing with his left. Beside him are the three girls (and their father) who, according to the legend, were brought onto the right path through the help the Saint gave them. In the background (on clouds) are Jesus and the Mother of God.

Saint Nicholas, or “the Wonderworker”, celebrated by Christians on 6 December, lived in the late 3rd and early 4th centuries. He was born into a wealthy family in Patara, in the province of Lycia, in the Asian part of today's Turkey. From childhood he showed exceptional faith, and in his youth he stood out for his fine conduct, fasting, discernment and intense spiritual life. He studied at the best schools, where he stood out for his intelligence, and in the churches he entered he amazed everyone with his gentleness and nobility of soul.
Since his uncle was bishop of Patara, Nicholas spent some time at the monastery there, where he became a priest.
Saint Nicholas worked miracles even during his lifetime. On a journey to the Holy Land, a violent storm frightened those on the ship, but Nicholas urged everyone to pray to God, and the storm stopped.
At the same time, Saint Nicholas raised a young sailor who had fallen from the mast and drowned. In Alexandria, too, Saint Nicholas healed many who were sick or possessed.
He saved the city of Myra (also in Lycia) from famine by appearing in a dream to an Italian merchant and urging him to come and sell his wheat there.
Because of the miracles he worked, Saint Nicholas is considered the protector of children, especially poor children, and also of sailors, bakers, unmarried girls and the unjustly accused.

Saint Nicholas is celebrated on 6 December by both the Orthodox and the Roman Catholic Church.

The relics of Saint Nicholas are kept in the Basilica of Bari, in Italy, in a crypt from which a colourless liquid flows, called “Manna” or “Holy Manna”. According to tradition, the bishop of this diocese mixes this liquid with water, blesses it and gives it to the faithful.
Part of the relics of Saint Nicholas are at the church of Saint George the New in Bucharest, at kilometre zero. Many places of worship also bear the name of Saint Nicholas.
